# Diagnosing Overheating on a 2002 Dodge Ram 1500: Beyond the Cooling System

You have a 2002 Dodge Ram 1500 with a 4.7L V8 engine, and it is overheating. You've already taken significant steps to address the issue by replacing the entire cooling system, specifically swapping out the condenser cooling fan because it fails to engage when engine temperatures rise, only activating when the AC is turned on. You've also replaced all relevant relays, yet the symptom persists without generating any OBD-II fault codes or illuminating the check engine light. This scenario suggests a classic case where the hardware replacement has isolated the problem but not solved it, pointing your attention toward the Engine Control Module (ECM).

However, before concluding that the computer is at fault, you must rigorously verify the electrical architecture of the fan circuit. The fact that the fan engages with AC activation confirms the motor itself likely spins and the primary power path from the battery to the fan is intact. The issue lies in the transition logic between the engine thermal state and the fan activation. In many GM and Dodge platforms of this era, including the 4.7L V8, the ECM controls the low-speed fan via a dedicated driver circuit inside the module. If that internal driver has failed, the ECM will not output the voltage required to close the relay coil, resulting in no fan operation during high-load thermal events, even if the external relays are new.

The absence of fault codes is a critical data point here. Modern ECMs monitor their own output drivers. If the ECM detects an open circuit on the fan control wire or a failure in its internal driver transistor, it typically sets a specific PID (Powertrain Diagnostic Trouble Code) related to the cooling fan system. The lack of these codes implies one of two possibilities: either the ECM is not attempting to drive the fan at all due to a missing input signal from the coolant temperature sensor, or the ECM's logic for determining "overheat" conditions is not being triggered correctly.

Consider the Coolant Temperature Sensor (CTS). If the resistance value read by the ECM does not drop below the threshold required to trigger fan duty cycle 1, the ECM assumes the engine is running cool and will not activate the fan. A faulty CTS that reads falsely low temperatures would mimic a healthy system until thermal stress causes a boil-over, at which point you might see overheating without code storage if the event is transient or if the sensor fails in an open-circuit manner that doesn't trigger a specific threshold monitor.

To verify this without immediately swapping the expensive ECM, you can use a multimeter to probe the control wire leading to the fan relay while monitoring coolant temperature. If the wire remains at battery voltage (12V) when the engine is hot and the AC is off, but drops to ground or fluctuates when the AC is on, the ECM is likely sending the signal correctly. If the wire stays dead regardless of AC status, you have a wiring harness issue upstream of the relay or an internal ECM driver failure.

Another potential pitfall involves the thermal overload protector built into the fan motor itself. Even if the fan spins with AC, the thermal switch inside may be tripped due to a previous overheating event where the fan was completely inoperative. If the motor windings are damaged or the centrifugal clutch is seized, replacing the fan assembly will not restore function until the unit is bench-tested for continuity and resistance across the terminals.

Finally, check the ECM power supply grounds. A corroded ground strap between the engine block and the chassis can cause erratic behavior in the cooling system logic, preventing the ECM from accurately reading sensor inputs or driving outputs reliably. Ensure all ground points near the EGR valve and the ECM are clean and tight. If you have ruled out the CTS, the wiring harness continuity, the fan motor thermal switch, and the ECM grounds, then the ECM itself becomes the most probable culprit. At that stage, you would need to compare the live data stream of the coolant temperature sensor against the physical temperature using a scan tool or infrared thermometer to confirm if the sensor reporting is accurate before condemning the module.
